title: IP Addresses: What Computers Actually Use
content:
You just learned that a domain is a human-readable label. Now let's talk about what's underneath it.

**What is an IP address?**

An IP address (Internet Protocol address) is a numerical label assigned to every device connected to the internet. It is what computers actually use to route traffic to each other.

When you type 'meridian-financial.com' into your browser, your computer translates that name into an IP address — something like 104.22.7.45 — and then uses that number to actually send and receive data. The domain name was for you. The IP address is for the network.

There are two formats currently in use:

**IPv4**: The original format. Four numbers separated by dots, each between 0 and 255. Example: 192.168.1.1 or 104.22.7.45. There are approximately 4.3 billion possible IPv4 addresses — far fewer than the number of internet-connected devices in existence today. IPv4 is the format you will work with most in reconnaissance.

**IPv6**: The newer format, designed to solve the address shortage. Eight groups of four hexadecimal characters separated by colons. Example: 2606:4700:20::681c:72d. There are 340 undecillion possible IPv6 addresses — effectively unlimited. Adoption is growing but IPv4 remains dominant in most corporate environments.

**Why the domain-to-IP mapping matters in investigation**

Here is where this gets interesting from a security perspective.

**One IP address can serve many domains.** This is called virtual hosting — a single server responds to requests for hundreds of different domains, routing each request to the right content based on the 'Host' header in the HTTP request. A shared hosting environment, for example, might host thousands of websites on a single IP.

This means: if you know the IP address of a server, you can reverse-lookup all the domains that point to it. This is called reverse DNS lookup. If a suspicious domain shares an IP with twenty other domains all registered within the same week, all pointing to the same Eastern European host — that is a strong indicator of a coordinated attack infrastructure.

**One domain can resolve to many IPs.** Load balancers and Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) use this to distribute traffic globally. A query for 'google.com' returns different IP addresses depending on where in the world you are — different CDN nodes serve different regions. The domain is constant; the IP varies.

**The CDN problem — the most important thing to understand here**

Many large organisations place their internet presence behind a CDN like Cloudflare, Akamai, or AWS CloudFront. This means the IP address you get when you look up their domain belongs to the CDN provider — not to the target organisation.

Cloudflare's IP ranges (starting with 104.16.x.x and 172.64.x.x, among others) are well known. If an A record resolves to one of these, you are looking at Cloudflare's infrastructure, not the target's servers.

But here is the critical point: the target's actual servers — their origin servers — still have real IP addresses. Finding those origin IPs behind the CDN is a classic passive reconnaissance challenge. Common approaches:

— **MX records**: Mail servers communicate directly without CDN proxying. The mail server IP often belongs to the target's real hosting environment.
— **Historical DNS records**: Before they added the CDN, what IP did the domain point to? Historical DNS services preserve these records.
— **Subdomains**: Development and staging environments are frequently not routed through the CDN and resolve directly to real server IPs.
— **Certificate Transparency**: Subdomains discovered through CT logs may resolve directly to origin IPs.

**The professional chain**

When Maya investigates Meridian Financial's domain, the chain is:

1. Domain → DNS A record → IP address (where does this domain point right now?)
2. IP address → IP WHOIS → IP block owner (who owns this IP — Cloudflare, AWS, or Meridian themselves?)
3. IP block owner → ASN lookup → all IP ranges owned by that organisation (what is the complete scope of their internet-facing infrastructure?)

Each step answers a different question. Together, they build a complete picture of who owns what — before a single packet reaches the target.

callouts.title: Private vs Public IP Addresses
callouts.text:
Not all IP addresses are reachable from the public internet. Private IP ranges are reserved for internal networks and cannot be routed across the internet:
— 10.0.0.0 to 10.255.255.255
— 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255
— 192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255

If you encounter one of these ranges in a DNS record or error message, the system is behind a private network. Internal IP addresses sometimes leak in error messages, HTTP response headers, and misconfigured APIs — which is itself a finding in a professional engagement.

callouts.title: Never Scan Until You Check IP Ownership
callouts.text: Before any active scanning, always verify that the IP address in the A record actually belongs to the target — not a CDN provider. Scanning a Cloudflare IP without authorisation is not scanning the target: it is scanning Cloudflare's infrastructure, which is outside your scope, outside your authorisation, and potentially a legal issue. IP WHOIS first. Always.

keyTerms.definition: A numerical label assigned to every internet-connected device, used to route traffic across the network. IPv4 uses four decimal numbers separated by dots. IPv6 uses hexadecimal groups separated by colons. The number computers actually use — domain names are a human-readable layer on top.

A technique where a single server with one IP address hosts multiple domain names simultaneously. The server uses the HTTP 'Host' header to determine which domain's content to serve. Enables reverse IP lookup — finding all domains hosted on a given IP address.

A globally distributed network of servers (Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly, AWS CloudFront) that sits in front of a target's actual infrastructure. CDN IPs belong to the provider, not the target. Finding the origin IP behind a CDN — the real server — is a standard passive reconnaissance challenge.
